paragraph.text: I33. "A shock collar is just a stimulus; it doesn't hurt the dog"

a shock collar works because the stimulus is unpleasant: if it didn't bother the dog, it wouldn't stop barking. And it doesn't treat the cause of the barking, which is usually boredom, fear, separation anxiety or lack of exercise. A 2020 study compared training with an electronic collar to reward-based training and found no advantage for the collar; reward-based training had better results for some commands. Another 2020 study found more signs of stress in dogs trained with aversive methods. The alternative recommended by veterinary associations is reward-based training (positive reinforcement), not punishment or violence. Wales banned these collars in 2010, and England in 2024.

P1 is true. P2 may be true in the short term. P3 is self-contradictory: if the stimulus weren't aversive, it wouldn't work. And the conclusion ignores alternatives that treat the cause.

A dog barks for a reason: because it's alone, scared, bored or wants to play. A shock collar gives it a nasty fright every time it barks, but it doesn't fix what it's feeling. It's better to find out why it barks and help, with walks, games and company. And to teach, the best way is to reward what it does right, with treats, cuddles and play, not to frighten, shout or hit.

Links the stimulus to whatever causes fear
The collar reduces barking because the dog learns to avoid an unpleasant stimulus. Calling it "just a stimulus" doesn't change how it works.
Barking is a symptom. Punishing it can silence the dog without solving the fear, boredom or anxiety, and can worsen its emotional state.

text.bold: 3. Reward-based training works as well or better.

paragraph.text: China, Mills and Cooper compared, in 2020, training with an electronic collar to other methods, with 63 dogs. The reward-based group responded better to some commands, and the authors found no advantage for the collar. Other researchers criticized limitations of the study.

text.bold: 4. The recommended alternative is reward-based training, not punishment or violence.

paragraph.text: Reward-based training (positive reinforcement) teaches the dog to do what's wanted and rewards success with food, play or affection, instead of punishing mistakes with shocks, jerks, shouting or smacks. A Portuguese study from 2020, with 92 dogs from training schools, found that dogs trained with aversive methods showed more stress behaviors during training, larger increases in cortisol and more "pessimistic" responses in a cognitive bias test, which measures emotional state, than dogs trained with rewards. Veterinary associations point the same way: the American Veterinary Society of Animal Behavior (AVSAB) recommends only reward-based methods for all training, including for behavior problems, and says there's no evidence that aversive methods are more effective; the British Small Animal Veterinary Association (BSAVA) recommends positive reinforcement and opposes aversive methods such as shock collars. Some trainers defend electronic collars, and research on the topic has limitations, but these bodies' consensus is clear.
Wales banned shock collars in 2010, and England in February 2024.

The question is whether it's fair to cause an animal discomfort to solve our own annoyance, without addressing what it's feeling. When there are methods that work without pain, the choice is clear.

It's true that excessive barking causes real conflicts, that guardians can feel they have no way out, and that the collar reduces barking in the short term.
But it works through discomfort, doesn't treat the cause, and there are methods that work without pain. The barking problem deserves to be solved from the dog's side.
